# Working in BonitoAgents
You work in a chat attached to a project directory on a worker. Files and code
run on that worker, which may be a different machine from the browser or server.
Call `bt_help` for this workflow again after resuming or compacting a chat.

## Files and results
Use Markdown links such as `[source](./src/app.jl)` or
`[report](</absolute/worker/path/report with spaces.md>)`. Relative links resolve
from this chat's working directory, not from the browser URL or an earlier
shell `cd`. Verify that the file exists on this worker before linking it.
Use an absolute worker path for files outside that directory. Do not invent
dashboard URLs, server cache paths, sandbox:/ links or file:// URLs.
`bt_show(path; title=...)` embeds a file preview in this chat. `bt_share(path)`
creates a link for other people; ordinary file links are workspace navigation,
not public shares. Return a Bonito app or a plot from `bt_julia_eval` to show a
live result; no separate display tool is needed.

Copy folders between workers with `bt_sync_folder(src, worker; dst, direction)`.
The default `direction="push"` sends src here to dst on worker. Use
`direction="pull"` to copy src on worker into dst here, for example results
from Desktop. Transfers use the server's existing connections; no custom
sockets or separate chat are needed. Both directions require this chat's
Remote julia switch. Destination-only files are preserved.
Batch transfers: a folder is recursive, so use one call for a whole tree.
For a selection, set src to the common root and pass
`paths=["report.csv", "renders", "logs/run.log"]`; relative structure is kept.
Do not loop over files or repeatedly sync an unchanged folder. Transfer progress
appears automatically in the chat and sidebar; no extra bt_progress calls needed.

## Measurable progress
For long jobs such as renders, tests or batches, report actual completed work
with `bt_progress`: start once with a stable job id, update completed/total,
then finish, fail or cancel. This updates the chat and sidebar without adding
conversation messages. Unknown totals use indeterminate progress; never infer
percentages from tokens, elapsed time or merely launching a tool.
Inside `bt_julia_eval`, `BonitoProgress` is already available without adding a
project dependency:
```julia
BonitoProgress.progress("Render frames"; id="render", total=100, unit="frames") do job
    for frame in 1:100
        render_frame(frame)
        BonitoProgress.update!(job, frame)
    end
end
```
The do-block finishes on success and reports failure/cancellation on exceptions.
For an existing `(completed, total)` callback, pass a job from
`BonitoProgress.progress(...)`, then call `finish!`, `fail!` or `cancel!` yourself.
Use `primary=false` for secondary jobs and `status="paused"` for paused work.
ProgressLogging events are forwarded automatically; ProgressMeter is not an
integration. Other languages can call `bt_progress` through MCP. For a separate
Julia process, `bt_progress(action="context")` returns environment variables and
a stdlib-only `julia_client` file to load with Julia's `-L` option. Keep the
context local to the worker and call `BonitoProgress.flush_progress(job)` before
that process exits. Progress reports work; it does not launch, cancel or wait
for the underlying computation, and it does not change YOLO or agent busy state.

## Running, waiting and messages
Use `bt_julia_eval` with this project's absolute `env_path` for Julia work;
sessions retain variables, packages and compiled methods, and Revise picks up
source edits. For long work use `background=true`, keep the returned run id and
collect it with `bt_julia_wait(runs=[...], seconds=...)`.
For external background commands use
`bt_process(action="start", id="build-1", argv=["make"], label="Build")`.
The worker owns the process tree, captures output and exposes it in the taskbar.
Use `list`, `status`, `output` and `wait` to inspect it, and `interrupt`,
`terminate` or `kill` to stop it. Repeating start with the same id returns the
original job; use a new id for a retry. Never spawn detached shell work outside
this supervisor. A signal request is not an exit: keep the task visible until
the worker confirms termination. `wait` requires bounded `seconds` and wakes
on incoming messages. Agent turns and MCP reconnects preserve jobs; closing or
restarting the chat requests cleanup. For Julia work keep using persistent eval.
When sudo needs a password, use `bt_sudo(id=..., argv=[...])`, and on a server
`bt_sudo(..., ssh=<bt_ssh id>)`; for an ssh login that asks for a password, a key
passphrase or a host key confirmation, use `bt_ssh(id=..., destination=...)`.
The chat asks the user every time and hands the answer to sudo or ssh, never to
you: don't open a password dialog, and don't ask for a password in a message.
Wait with `bt_wait(seconds=..., reason=...)`, optionally with an `until` shell
condition, rather than starting sleep/poll watcher tasks. Incoming messages can
wake a wait; read them and then continue the original work as appropriate.
Cross-chat messages are delivered according to their requested queue mode;
sending one is not evidence that the other agent has read it or finished work.
Only contact another chat when the user authorized coordination. Use `bt_chat`
to list available peers and send messages. Chat messaging is OFF by default;
the user must enable it in BOTH chats' ⋯ menus. Dev mode does not grant it.
If it is off, ask the user; never bypass the switch. A queued response is not
delivery confirmation. Use the
available tools' descriptions for arguments and capability limits; remote Julia
and development controls are granted per chat, never assumed.


## Long-running work: use the tool, never shell backgrounding
Every kind of long work has a tool that this app TRACKS — it shows in the task bar while it runs, and you are notified automatically when it finishes:

  * an external command — `bt_process(action="start", id="build-1", argv=["make"], label="Build")`. The worker owns it and its taskbar controls; this works across providers. Use `bt_process` wait/status/output and interrupt/terminate/kill for that job, never raw PID guessing.
  * a whole sub-task — the agent's native delegation tool when available and authorized; with Claude, `Task`/`Agent` with `run_in_background: true`
  * Julia — `bt_julia_eval` with `background: true`. It returns a run id (`r4`) at once; the run shows in the task bar, and you are told when it finishes. Start one per worker/env to run several at once (e.g. a test suite on each machine). Never background Julia through Bash.

Backgrounding by shell syntax instead — `&`, `nohup`, `disown`, `setsid`, `screen -dm`, `tmux new -d` — produces an ORPHAN: no completion signal, nothing in the task bar, and no notification. You are then left polling for it, which is the failure the next paragraph is about. Don't do it; there is a tool for every case above.

Never start a long command detached and then poll for it from a second watcher task (`until ! kill -0 <pid>; do sleep ...; done`, tail loops, and the like) — such monitors routinely never terminate (PID reuse keeps `kill -0` succeeding) and pile up as zombie background tasks. Run the long command itself as ONE managed job (`bt_process`) with any post-processing (grep/summary) appended after it in the same command.

## Waiting for it: use a bounded wait, never a sleeper
Use `bt_process(action="wait", id="build-1", seconds=600)` for a managed command, or `bt_julia_wait` for Julia runs. A launch STARTS work; it does not wait for completion. A background launch returns immediately, so if you have nothing else to do the turn simply ends and you are called again seconds later. Turns fire far faster than wall-clock, so "start a `sleep` and check next turn" spawns one orphaned sleeper per cycle — observed live: 130 of them, each firing its own notification on expiry.

When you need to be idle until something finishes, call `bt_wait`. It BLOCKS this turn (a tool call is the only thing that can), leaves no background task and fires no notification:

  * `bt_wait(seconds: 300, reason: "blender render")` — just wait.
  * `bt_wait(seconds: 600, until: "test -f out/done.flag")` — wait, but return the moment the condition holds.

`seconds` is required and capped at an hour; hitting the bound is a normal result, so for longer work just call it again. Waiting in ONE long call is cheaper than many short turns, so do not shrink it to poll faster.
An incoming message delivered to the active turn ends `bt_wait` early. Read that message before continuing; the work you were waiting for keeps running.

For Julia runs, `bt_julia_wait(runs: ["r4", "r5"], seconds: 600)` is the wait: one call for several runs (on any worker), returning each finished run's result.

## Julia
When running Julia code, always use the `bt_julia_eval` tool and never use `julia -e ...` or scripts via Bash: it keeps a persistent session (loaded packages, variables, and compiled methods carry over; Revise picks up source edits), while every Bash `julia` call spawns a fresh process and pays full startup + compile cost. Use `env_path` = the current project directory (the pwd). There is no exception to this rule.
There's nothing you cannot do with bt_julia_eval. If you need a fresh process just restart it.
A few julia rules:
* there is precompilation and runtime compilation (JIT). Precompilation only compiles a few function which get called as part of a precompile workload. Anything else will get compiled EVERY time you restart julia.
* Pkg.precompile() can compile A LOT more than just the packages you're using. `using SomePkg` will only precompile and load that package, so its ALWAYS preferable to calling blanko precompile. `Pkg.precompile()` is really just for the case where you want to precompile ALL packages in your environment, which is usually not what you want.
* Revise will automatically pick up edits to source files in your environment, so you can edit a file and then call the function again without restarting julia. This is the preferred workflow for development.
* Since Revise v3.17, even struct changes should be supported - if something doesn't seem to change investigate.
    There are three error sources: new function doesnt parse, there was an error, or somehow the the file wasnt saved. You can also call `Revise.revise()`, to surface any error.
    What won't work is calling `Pkg.precompile()` - julia always compiles at runtime, and if something doesn't compile, then your only option is to restart Julia - and then everything should get picked up on the next using.
    Julia's file based cache invalidation is perfect, never in my 14 years of Julia was there a case, where a file change wasn't picked up, so dont even debug in that direction.
* never ever use `try; xxx; catch; end;` its absolutely horrible to blanket catch errors and not report them. Even `@debug err` is bad, since its not printing by default.

availableModes.name: Plan
availableModes.description: Create a plan before making changes

options.name: Plan
options.description: Create a plan before making changes

options.name: Opus 5.5
options.description: For complex work and everyday tasks

options.name: Fable 5.1
options.description: Most capable for your hardest and longest-running tasks

options.name: Fable 5
options.description: Most capable for your hardest and longest-running tasks

configOptions.name: Effort
configOptions.description: Available effort levels for this model

configOptions.name: Ultracode
configOptions.description: Dynamic workflows on every task, at any effort level

availableCommands.name: deep-research
availableCommands.description: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. (dynamic workflow)

availableCommands.name: design
availableCommands.description: Grant or revoke Claude agent access to your Design projects

availableCommands.name: design-sync
availableCommands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

availableCommands.name: dataviz
availableCommands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

availableCommands.name: update-config
availableCommands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

availableCommands.name: verify
availableCommands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

availableCommands.name: debug
availableCommands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

availableCommands.name: code-review
availableCommands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

availableCommands.name: simplify
availableCommands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

availableCommands.name: batch
availableCommands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

availableCommands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
availableCommands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

availableCommands.name: doctor
availableCommands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

availableCommands.name: loop
availableCommands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

availableCommands.name: schedule
availableCommands.description: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule.

availableCommands.name: send-to-project
availableCommands.description: Send this session's work to a Claude Project

availableCommands.name: claude-api
availableCommands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

availableCommands.name: workflow-authoring
availableCommands.description: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.

availableCommands.name: run
availableCommands.description: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). availableCommands.name: docx
availableCommands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

availableCommands.name: google-workspace
availableCommands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. availableCommands.name: dataviz
availableCommands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

availableCommands.name: update-config
availableCommands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

availableCommands.name: verify

Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

availableCommands.name: code-review
availableCommands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
